entries.7c13fb3481bc67314ce23daa6ee24208cfcdb7c8: <div sID="gen17824" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="29" osisID="Jer.29" sID="Jer.29"/> <div eID="gen17824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17825" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17826" type="x-p"/> The contest between Jeremiah and the false prophets was carried on before by preaching, here by writing; there we had sermon against sermon, here we have letter against letter, for some of the false prophets are now carried away into captivity in Babylon, while Jeremiah remains in his own country. Now here is, I. A letter which Jeremiah wrote to the captives in Babylon, against their prophets that they had there (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.1-Jer.29.3">ver. 1-3</reference>), in which letter, 1. He endeavours to reconcile them to their captivity, to be easy under it and to make the best of it, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.4-Jer.29.7">ver. 4-7</reference>. 2. He cautions them not to give any credit to their false prophets, who fed them with hopes of a speedy release, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.8-Jer.29.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. 3. He assures them that God would restore them in mercy to their own land again, at the end of 70 years, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10-Jer.29.14">ver. 10-14</reference>. 4. He foretels the destruction of those who yet continued, and that they should be persecuted with one judgment after another, and sent at last into captivity, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.15-Jer.29.19">ver. 15-19</reference>. 5. He prophesies the destruction of two of their false prophets that they had in Babylon, that both soothed them up in their sins and set them bad examples (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.20-Jer.29.23">ver. 20-23</reference>), and this is the purport of Jeremiah's letter. II. Here is a letter which Shemaiah, a false prophet in Babylon, wrote to the priests at Jerusalem, to stir them up to persecute Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.24-Jer.29.29">ver. 24-29</reference>), and a denunciation of God's wrath against him for writing such a letter, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.30-Jer.29.32">ver. 30-32</reference>. Such struggles as these have there always been between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent.
entries.763d8be9c4306521a1b869fe2bd91ada65df8816: <div eID="gen17826" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17825" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Advice to the Captives in Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 596.)</title> <div sID="gen17827" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem unto the residue of the elders which were carried away captives, and to the priests, and to the prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon; <hi type="super">2</hi> (After that Jeconiah the king, and the queen, and the eunuchs, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem, and the carpenters, and the smiths, were departed from Jerusalem;) <hi type="super">3</hi> By the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan, and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent unto Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon) saying, <hi type="super">4</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel, unto all that are carried away captives, whom I have caused to be carried away from Jerusalem unto Babylon; <hi type="super">5</hi> Build ye houses, and dwell <hi type="italic">in them;</hi> and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them; <hi type="super">6</hi> Take ye wives, and beget sons and daughters; and take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters; that ye may be increased there, and not diminished. <hi type="super">7</hi> And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace. <div eID="gen17827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17828" type="x-p"/> We are here told, <div eID="gen17828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17829" type="x-p"/> I. That Jeremiah wrote to the captives in Babylon, in the name of the Lord. Jeconiah had surrendered himself a prisoner, with the queen his mother, the chamberlains of his household, called here the <hi type="italic">eunuchs,</hi> and many of <hi type="italic">the princes of Judah and Jerusalem,</hi> who were at that time the most active men; <hi type="italic">the carpenters and smiths</hi> likewise, being demanded, were yielded up, that those who remained might not have any proper hands to fortify their city or furnish themselves with weapons of war. By this tame submission it was hoped that Nebuchadnezzar would be pacified. <hi type="italic">Satis est prostrasse leoni—It suffices the lion to have laid his antagonist prostrate;</hi> but the imperious conqueror grows upon their concessions, like Benhadad upon Ahab's, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.5-1Kgs.20.6">1 Kings xx. 5, 6</reference>. And, not content with this, when these had <hi type="italic">departed from Jerusalem</hi> he comes again, and fetches away many more of <hi type="italic">the elders, the priests, the prophets, and the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.1">v. 1</reference>), such as he thought fit, or such as his soldiers could lay hands on, and carries them to Babylon. The case of these captives was very melancholy, the rather because they, being thus distinguished from the rest of their brethren who continued in their own land, looked as if they were greater sinners than all men who dwelt at Jerusalem. Jeremiah therefore writes a letter to them, to comfort them, assuring them that they had no reason either to despair of succour themselves or to envy their brethren that were left behind. Note, 1. The word of God written is as truly given by <hi type="italic">inspiration of God</hi> as his word spoken was; and this was the proper way of spreading the knowledge of God's will among his <hi type="italic">children scattered abroad.</hi> 2. We may serve God and do good by writing to our friends at a distance pious letters of seasonable comforts and wholesome counsels. Those whom we cannot speak to we may write to; that which is written remains. This letter of Jeremiah's was sent to the captives in Babylon by the hands of the ambassadors whom king Zedekiah sent to Nebuchadnezzar, probably to pay him his tribute and renew his submission to him, or to treat of peace with him, in which treaty the captives might perhaps hope that they should be included, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.3">v. 3</reference>. By such messengers Jeremiah chose to send this message, to put an honour upon it, because it was a message from God, or perhaps because there was no settled way of sending letters to Babylon, but as such an occasion as this offered, and then it made the condition of the captives there the more melancholy, that they could rarely hear from their friends and relations they had left behind, which is some reviving and satisfaction to those that are separated from one another. <div eID="gen17829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17830" type="x-p"/> II. We are here told what he wrote. A copy of the letter at large follows here to <reference osisRef="Jer.29.24">v. 24</reference>. In these verses, <div eID="gen17830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17831" type="x-p"/> 1. He assures them that he wrote in the name of the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts, the God of Israel,</hi> who indited the letter; Jeremiah was but the scribe or amanuensis. It would be comfortable to them, in their captivity, to hear that God is <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> of all hosts, and is therefore able to help and deliver them; and that he is the <hi type="italic">God of Israel</hi> still, a God in covenant with his people, though he contend with them, and their enemies for the present are too hard for them. This would likewise be an admonition to them to stand upon their guard against all temptations to the idolatry of Babylon, because the <hi type="italic">God of Israel,</hi> the God whom they served, is <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts.</hi> God's sending to them in this letter might be an encouragement to them in their captivity, as it was an evidence that he had not cast them off, had not abandoned them and disinherited them, though he was displeased with them and corrected them; for, if the Lord had been pleased to kill them, he would not have written to them. <div eID="gen17831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17832" type="x-p"/> 2. God by him owns the hand he had in their captivity: <hi type="italic">I have caused you to be carried away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.29.4">v. 4</reference> and again, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.7">v. 7</reference>. All the force of the king of Babylon could not have done it if God had not ordered it; nor could he have any power against them but what was given him from above. If God caused them to be carried captives, they might be sure that he neither did them any wrong nor meant them any hurt. Note, It will help very much to reconcile us to our troubles, and to make us patient under them, to consider that they are what God has appointed us to. <hi type="italic">I opened not my mouth, because thou didst it.</hi> <div eID="gen17832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17833" type="x-p"/> 3. He bids them think of nothing but settling there; and therefore let them resolve to make the best of it (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.5-Jer.29.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Build yourselves houses and dwell in them,</hi> &c. By all this it is intimated to them, (1.) That they must not feed themselves with hopes of a speedy return out of their captivity, for that would keep them still unsettled and consequently uneasy; they would apply themselves to no business, take no comfort, but be always tiring themselves and provoking their conquerors with the expectations of relief; and their disappointment at last would sink them into despair and make their condition much more miserable than otherwise it would be. Let them therefore reckon upon a continuance there, and accommodate themselves to it as well as they can. Let them <hi type="italic">build,</hi> and <hi type="italic">plant,</hi> and <hi type="italic">marry,</hi> and dispose of their children there as if they were at home in their own land. Let them take a pleasure in seeing their families built up and multiplied; for, though they must expect themselves to die in captivity, yet their children may live to see better days. If they live in the fear of God, what should hinder them but they may live comfortably in Babylon? They cannot but <hi type="italic">weep</hi> sometimes <hi type="italic">when they remember Zion.</hi> But let not weeping hinder sowing; let them not <hi type="italic">sorrow as those that have no hope,</hi> no joy; for they have both. Note, In all conditions of life it is our wisdom and duty to make the best of that which is, and not to throw away the comfort of what we may have because we have not all we would have. We have a natural affection for our native country; it strangely draws our minds; but it is with a <hi type="italic">nescio qua dulcedine—we can give no good account of the sweet attraction;</hi> and therefore, if providence remove us to some other country, we must resolve to live easy there, to bring our mind to our condition when our condition is not in every thing to our mind. If the <hi type="italic">earth be the Lord's,</hi> then, wherever a child of God goes, he does not go off his Father's ground. <hi type="italic">Patria est ubicunque bene est—That place is our country in which we are well off.</hi> If things be not as they have been, instead of fretting at that, we must live in hopes that they will be better than they are. <hi type="italic">Non si male nunc, et olim sic erit—Though we suffer now we shall not always.</hi> (2.) That they must not disquiet themselves with fears of intolerable hardships in their captivity. They might be ready to suggest (as persons in trouble are always apt to make the worst of things) that it would be in vain to build houses, for their lords and masters would not suffer them to dwell in them when they had built them, nor to eat the fruit of the vineyards they planted. "Never fear," says God; "if you live peaceably with them, you shall find them civil to you." Meek and quiet people, that work and mind their own business, have often found much better treatment, even with strangers and enemies, than they expected; and God has made his people to be <hi type="italic">pitied of those that carry them captives</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.46">Ps. cvi. 46</reference>), and a pity it is but that those who have built houses should dwell in them. Nay, <div eID="gen17833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17834" type="x-p"/> 4. He directs them to seek the good of the country where they were captives (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.7">v. 7</reference>), to pray for it, to endeavour to promote it. This forbids them to attempt any thing against the public peace while they were subjects to the king of Babylon. Though he was a heathen, an idolater, an oppressor, and an enemy to God and his church, yet, while he gave them protection, they must pay him allegiance, and live <hi type="italic">quiet and peaceable lives</hi> under him, <hi type="italic">in all godliness and honesty,</hi> not plotting to shake off his yoke, but patiently leaving it to God in due time to work deliverance for them. Nay, they must pray to God for the peace of the places where they were, that they might oblige them to continue their kindness to them and disprove the character that had been given their nation, that they were <hi type="italic">hurtful to kings and provinces,</hi> and <hi type="italic">moved sedition,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.15">Ezra iv. 15</reference>. Both the wisdom of the serpent and the innocency of the dove required them to be true to the government they lived under: <hi type="italic">For in the peace thereof you shall have peace;</hi> should the country be embroiled in war, they would have the greatest share in the calamitous effects of it. Thus the primitive Christians, according to the temper of their holy religion, prayed for the powers that were, though they were persecuting powers. And, if they were to pray for and seek the peace of the land of their captivity, much more reason have we to pray for the welfare of the land of our nativity, where we are a free people under a good government, <hi type="italic">that in the peace thereof</hi> we and ours <hi type="italic">may have peace.</hi> Every passenger is concerned in the safety of the ship.
entries.620ea564ffa0797c902a45f9f215e58534a3b614: <div eID="gen17834" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Advice to the Captives in Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 596.)</title> <div sID="gen17835" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Let not your prophets and your diviners, that <hi type="italic">be</hi> in the midst of you, deceive you, neither hearken to your dreams which ye cause to be dreamed. <hi type="super">9</hi> For they prophesy falsely unto you in my name: I have not sent them, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">10</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place. <hi type="super">11</hi> For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then shall ye call upon me, and ye shall go and pray unto me, and I will hearken unto you. <hi type="super">13</hi> And ye shall seek me, and find <hi type="italic">me,</hi> when ye shall search for me with all your heart. <hi type="super">14</hi> And I will be found of you, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and I will turn away your captivity, and I will gather you from all the nations, and from all the places whither I have driven you, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and I will bring you again into the place whence I caused you to be carried away captive. <div eID="gen17835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17836" type="x-p"/> To make the people quiet and easy in their captivity, <div eID="gen17836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17837" type="x-p"/> I. God takes them off from building upon the false foundation which their pretended prophets laid, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.8-Jer.29.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. They told them that their captivity should be short, and therefore that they must not think of taking root in Babylon, but be upon the wing to go back: "Now herein <hi type="italic">they deceive you,</hi>" says God; "they <hi type="italic">prophesy a lie to you,</hi> though they prophesy <hi type="italic">in my name.</hi> But <hi type="italic">let them not deceive you,</hi> suffer not yourselves to be deluded by them." As long as we have the word of truth to try the spirits by it is our own fault if we be deceived; for by it we may be undeceived. <hi type="italic">Hearken not to your dreams, which you cause to be dreamed.</hi> He means either the dreams or fancies which the people pleased themselves with, and with which they filled their own heads (by thinking and speaking of nothing else but a speedy enlargement when they were awake they caused themselves to dream of it when they were asleep, and then took that for a good omen, and with it strengthened themselves in their vain expectations), or the dreams which the prophets dreamed and grounded their prophecies upon. God tells the people, <hi type="italic">They are your dreams,</hi> because they pleased them, were the dreams that they desired and wished for. They <hi type="italic">caused them to be dreamed;</hi> for they hearkened to them, and encouraged the prophets to put such deceits upon them, desiring them to prophesy nothing but <hi type="italic">smooth things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Isa. xxx. 10</reference>. They were dreams of their own bespeaking. False prophets would not flatter people in their sins, but that they love to be flattered, and speak smoothly to their prophets that their prophets may speak smoothly to them. <div eID="gen17837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17838" type="x-p"/> II. He gives them a good foundation to build their hopes upon. We would not persuade people to pull down the house they have built upon the sand, but that there is a rock ready for them to rebuild upon. God here promises them that, though they should not return quickly, they should return at length, <hi type="italic">after seventy years be accomplished.</hi> By this it appears that the seventy years of the captivity are not to be reckoned from the last captivity, but the first. Note, Though the deliverance of the church do not come in our time, it is sufficient that it will come in God's time, and we are sure that that is the best time. The promise is that God will visit them in mercy; though he had long seemed to be strange to them, he will come among them, and appear for them, and put honour upon them, as great men do upon their inferiors by coming to visit them. He will put an end to <hi type="italic">their captivity,</hi> and <hi type="italic">turn away</hi> all the calamities of it. Though they are dispersed, some in one country and some in another, he will <hi type="italic">gather them from all the places whither they are driven,</hi> will set up a standard for them all to resort to, and incorporate them again in one body. And though they are at a great distance they shall be brought again to their own land, <hi type="italic">to the place whence</hi> they were <hi type="italic">carried captive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.29.14">v. 14</reference>. Now, 1. This shall be the performance of God's promise to them (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will perform my good word towards you.</hi> Let not the failing of those predictions which are delivered as from God lessen the reputation of those that really are from him. That which is indeed God's word is a <hi type="italic">good word,</hi> and therefore it will be made good, and not one iota or tittle of it shall fall to the ground. <hi type="italic">Hath he said, and shall he not do it?</hi> This will make their return out of captivity very comfortable, that it will be the performance of God's good word to them, the product of a gracious promise. 2. This shall be in pursuance of God's purposes concerning them (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">I know the thoughts that I think towards you.</hi> Known unto God are all his works, for known unto him are all his thoughts (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.18">Acts xv. 18</reference>) and his works agree exactly with his thoughts; he does all <hi type="italic">according to the counsel of his will.</hi> We often do not know our own thoughts, nor know our own mind, but God is never at any uncertainty within himself. We are sometimes ready to fear that God's designs concerning us are all against us; but he knows the contrary concerning his own people, that they are <hi type="italic">thoughts of good and not of evil;</hi> even that which seems evil is designed for good. His thoughts are all working towards the expected end, which he will give in due time. The end they expect will come, though perhaps not when they expect it. Let them have patience till the fruit is ripe, and then they shall have it. He will give them <hi type="italic">an end, and expectation,</hi> so it is in the original. (1.) He will give them to see <hi type="italic">the end</hi> (the comfortable termination) of their trouble; though it last long, it shall not last always. The <hi type="italic">time to favour Zion,</hi> yea, the <hi type="italic">set time, will come.</hi> When things are at the worst they will begin to mend; and he will give them to see the glorious perfection of their deliverance; for, as for God, his work is perfect. He that in the beginning finished the <hi type="italic">heavens and the earth,</hi> and all the <hi type="italic">hosts</hi> of both, will finish all the blessings of both to his people. When he begins in ways of mercy he will <hi type="italic">make an end.</hi> God does nothing by halves. (2.) He will give them to see the <hi type="italic">expectation,</hi> that <hi type="italic">end</hi> which they desire and hope for, and have been long waiting for. He will give them, not the expectations of their fears, nor the expectations of their fancies, but the expectations of their faith, the end which he has promised and which will turn for the best to them. 3. This shall be in answer to their prayers and supplications to God, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.12-Jer.29.15">v. 12-14</reference>. (1.) God will stir them up to pray: <hi type="italic">Then shall you call upon me,</hi> and <hi type="italic">you shall go, and pray unto me.</hi> Note, When God is about to give his people the expected good he pours out a spirit of prayer, and it is a good sign that he is coming towards them in mercy. Then, when you see the <hi type="italic">expected end</hi> approaching, <hi type="italic">then you shall call upon me.</hi> Note, Promises are given, not to supersede, but to quicken and encourage prayer: and when deliverance is coming we must by prayer go forth to meet it. When Daniel understood that the 70 years were near expiring, then he <hi type="italic">set his face</hi> with more fervency than ever <hi type="italic">to seek the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.2-Dan.9.3">Dan. ix. 2, 3</reference>. (2.) He will then stir up himself to come and save them (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.2">Ps. lxxx. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will hearken unto you,</hi> and <hi type="italic">I will be found of you.</hi> God has said it, and we may depend upon it, <hi type="italic">Seek and you shall find.</hi> We have a general rule laid down (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall find me when you shall search for me with all your heart.</hi> In seeking God we must search for him, accomplish a diligent search, search for directions in seeking him and encouragements to our faith and hope. We must continue seeking, and take pains in seeking, as those that search; and this we must do with our heart (that is, in sincerity and uprightness), and with our whole heart (that is, with vigour and fervency, putting forth <hi type="italic">all that is within us</hi> in prayer), and those who thus <hi type="italic">seek God</hi> shall <hi type="italic">find him,</hi> and shall find him their bountiful rewarder, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.6">Heb. xi. 6</reference>. He never said to such, <hi type="italic">Seek you me in vain.</hi>
entries.a4916402d01ffa3304b46418ea13c537a3cbf62d: <div eID="gen17838" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of the False Prophets. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 596.)</title> <div sID="gen17839" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Because ye have said, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath raised us up prophets in Babylon; <hi type="super">16</hi> <hi type="italic">Know</hi> that thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of the king that sitteth upon the throne of David, and of all the people that dwelleth in this city, <hi type="italic">and</hi> of your brethren that are not gone forth with you into captivity; <hi type="super">17</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Behold, I will send upon them the sword, the famine, and the pestilence, and will make them like vile figs, that cannot be eaten, they are so evil. <hi type="super">18</hi> And I will persecute them with the sword, with the famine, and with the pestilence, and will deliver them to be removed to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a curse, and an astonishment, and a hissing, and a reproach, among all the nations whither I have driven them: <hi type="super">19</hi> Because they have not hearkened to my words, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which I sent unto them by my servants the prophets, rising up early and sending <hi type="italic">them;</hi> but ye would not hear, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">20</hi> Hear ye therefore the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all ye of the captivity, whom I have sent from Jerusalem to Babylon: <hi type="super">21</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel, of Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and of Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, which prophesy a lie unto you in my name; Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall slay them before your eyes; <hi type="super">22</hi> And of them shall be taken up a curse by all the captivity of Judah which <hi type="italic">are</hi> in Babylon, saying, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire; <hi type="super">23</hi> Because they have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours' wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them; even I know, and <hi type="italic">am</hi> a witness, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen17839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17840" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah, having given great encouragement to those among the captives whom he knew to be serious and well-affected, assuring them that God had very kind and favourable intentions concerning them, here turns to those among them who slighted the counsels and comforts that Jeremiah ministered to them and depended upon what the false prophets flattered them with. When this letter came from Jeremiah they would be ready to say, "Why should he make himself so busy, and take upon him to advise us? <hi type="italic">The Lord has raised us up prophets in Babylon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.29.15">v. 15</reference>. We are satisfied with those prophets, and can depend upon them, and have no occasion to hear from any prophets in Jerusalem." See the impudent wickedness of this people; as the prophets, when they prophesied lies, said that they had them from God, so the people, when they invited those prophets thus to flatter them, fathered it upon God, and said that it was the Lord that raised them up those prophets. Whereas we may be sure that those who harden people in their sins, and deceive them with false and groundless hopes of God's mercy, are no prophets of God's raising up. These prophets of their own told them that no more should be carried captive, but that those who were in captivity should shortly return. Now, in answer to this, 1. The prophet here foretells the utter destruction of those who remained still at Jerusalem, notwithstanding what those false prophets said to the contrary: "As for the <hi type="italic">king</hi> and <hi type="italic">people</hi> that <hi type="italic">dwell in the city,</hi> who, you think, will be ready to bid you welcome when you return, you are deceived; they shall be followed with one judgment after another, <hi type="italic">sword, famine,</hi> and <hi type="italic">pestilence,</hi> which shall cut off multitudes; and the poor and miserable remains shall be <hi type="italic">removed into all kingdoms of the earth,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Jer.29.16">v. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.18">18</reference>. And thus God <hi type="italic">will make them,</hi> or rather deal with them accordingly, as the salt that has <hi type="italic">lost its savour,</hi> which, being good for nothing, is cast to the dunghill, and so are rotten figs. This refers to the vision and the prophecy upon it which we had <reference osisRef="Jer.24.1-Jer.24.10">ch. xxiv.</reference> And the reason given for these proceedings against them is the same that has often been given and will justify God in the eternal ruin of impenitent sinners (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Because they have not hearkened to my words. I called, but they refused.</hi> 2. He foretells the judgment of God upon the false prophets in Babylon, who deceived the people of God there. He calls upon all the children of the captivity, who boasted of them as prophets of God's raising up (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.20">v. 20</reference>): "Stand still, and hear the doom of the prophets you are so fond of." The two prophets are named here, <hi type="italic">Ahab</hi> and <hi type="italic">Zedekiah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.29.21">v. 21</reference>. Observe, (1.) The crimes charged upon them—impiety and immorality: They <hi type="italic">prophesied lies in God's name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.21">v. 21</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.23">v. 23</reference>), They have <hi type="italic">spoken lying words in my name.</hi> Lying was bad, lying to the people of God to delude them into a false hope was worse, but fathering their lies upon the God of truth was worst of all. And no marvel if those that had the face to do that could allow themselves in the gratification of those vile affections to which God, in a way of righteous judgment, <hi type="italic">gave them up.</hi> They have done <hi type="italic">villainy in Israel,</hi> for <hi type="italic">they have committed adultery with their neighbours' wives.</hi> Adultery is villainy in Israel, and in such as pretend to be prophets, who by such wickednesses manifestly disprove their own pretensions. God never sent such profligate wretches on his errands. He is the <hi type="italic">Lord God of the holy prophets,</hi> not of such impure ones. Here it appears why they flattered others in their sins—because they could not reprove them without condemning themselves. These lewd practices of theirs they knew how to conceal from the eye of the world, that they might preserve their credit; but <hi type="italic">I know</hi> it <hi type="italic">and am a witness, saith the Lord.</hi> The most secret sins are known to God; he can see the villainy that is covered with the thickest cloak of hypocrisy, and there is a day coming when he will bring to light all these hidden works of darkness and every man will appear in his own colours. (2.) The judgments threatened against them: <hi type="italic">The king of Babylon shall slay them before your eyes;</hi> nay, he shall put them to a miserable death, <hi type="italic">roast them in the fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.29.22">v. 22</reference>. We may suppose that it was not for their impiety and immorality that Nebuchadnezzar punished them thus severely, but for sedition, and some attempts of their turbulent spirits upon the public peace, and stirring up the people to revolt and rebel. So much of their wickedness shall then be detected, and in such a wretched manner they shall end their days, that their names shall be a curse among the captives in Babylon, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.22">v. 22</reference>. When men would imprecate the greatest evil upon one they hated they would think they could not load them with a heavier curse, in fewer words, than to say, <hi type="italic">The Lord make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab.</hi> Thus were they made ashamed of the prophets they had been proud of, and convinced at last of their folly in hearkening to them. God's faithful prophets were sometimes charged with being the troublers of the land, and as such were tortured and slain; but their names were a blessing when they were gone and their memory sweet, not as these false prophets. As malefactors are attended with infamy and disgrace, so martyrs with glory and honour.
entries.ee940f435fe7b232562d4190bbdd1344ce4b86b2: <div eID="gen17840" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Malice of Shemaiah; The Doom of Shemaiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 596.)</title> <div sID="gen17841" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> <hi type="italic">Thus</hi> shalt thou also speak to Shemaiah the Nehelamite, saying, <hi type="super">25</hi> Thus speaketh the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel, saying, Because thou hast sent letters in thy name unto all the people that <hi type="italic">are</hi> at Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests, saying, <hi type="super">26</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath made thee priest in the stead of Jehoiada the priest, that ye should be officers in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , for every man <hi type="italic">that is</hi> mad, and maketh himself a prophet, that thou shouldest put him in prison, and in the stocks. <hi type="super">27</hi> Now therefore why hast thou not reproved Jeremiah of Anathoth, which maketh himself a prophet to you? <hi type="super">28</hi> For therefore he sent unto us <hi type="italic">in</hi> Babylon, saying, This <hi type="italic">captivity is</hi> long: build ye houses, and dwell <hi type="italic">in them;</hi> and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them. <hi type="super">29</hi> And Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the ears of Jeremiah the prophet. <hi type="super">30</hi> Then came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto Jeremiah, saying, <hi type="super">31</hi> Send to all them of the captivity, saying, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite; Because that Shemaiah hath prophesied unto you, and I sent him not, and he caused you to trust in a lie: <hi type="super">32</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Behold, I will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite, and his seed: he shall not have a man to dwell among this people; neither shall he behold the good that I will do for my people, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; because he hath taught rebellion against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen17841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17842" type="x-p"/> We have perused the contents of Jeremiah's letter to the captives in Babylon, who had reason, with a great deal of thanks to God and him, to acknowledge the receipt of it, and lay it up among their treasures. But we cannot wonder if the false prophets they had among them were enraged at it; for it gave them their true character. Now here we are told concerning one of them, <div eID="gen17842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17843" type="x-p"/> I. How he manifested his malice against Jeremiah. This busy fellow is called <hi type="italic">Shemaiah the Nehelamite,</hi> the <hi type="italic">dreamer</hi> (so the margin reads it), because all his prophecies he pretended to have received from God in a dream. He had got a copy of Jeremiah's letter to the captives, or had heard it read, or information was given to him concerning it, and it nettled him exceedingly; and he will take pen in hand, and answer it, yea, that he will. But how? He does not write to Jeremiah in justification of his own mission, nor offer any rational arguments for the support of his prophecies concerning the speedy return of the captives; but he writes to the priests, those faithful patrons of the false prophets, and instigates them to persecute Jeremiah. He writes in his own name, not so much as pretending to have the people's consent to it; but, as if he must be dictator to all mankind, he sends a circular letter (as it should seem) among the priests at Jerusalem and the rest of the people, probably by the same messengers that brought the letter from Jeremiah. But it is chiefly directed to Zephaniah, who was either the immediate son of Maaseiah, or of the 24th course of the priests, of which Maaseiah was the father and head. He was not the high priest, but sagan or suffragan to the high priest, or in some other considerable post of command in the temple, as Pashur, <reference osisRef="Jer.20.1">ch. xx. 1</reference>. Perhaps he was chairman of that committee of priests that was appointed in a particular manner to take cognizance of those that pretended to be prophets, of which there were very many at this time, and to give judgment concerning them. Now, 1. He puts him and the other priests in mind of the duty of their place (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord hath made thee priest instead of Jehoiada the priest.</hi> Some think that he refers to the famous Jehoiada, that great reformer in the days of Joash; and (says Mr. Gataker) he would insinuate that this Zephaniah is for spirit and zeal such another as he, and raised up, as he was, for the glory of God and the good of the church; and therefore it was expected from him that he should proceed against Jeremiah. Thus (says he) there is no act so injurious or impious, but that wicked wretches and false prophets will not only attempt it, but colour it also with some specious pretence of piety and zeal for God's glory, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.6">Isa. lxvi. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.2">John xvi. 2</reference>. Or, rather, it was some other Jehoiada, his immediate predecessor in this office, who perhaps was carried to Babylon among the priests, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.1">v. 1</reference>. Zephaniah is advanced, sooner than he expected, to this place of trust and power, and Shemaiah would have him think that Providence had preferred him that he might persecute God's prophets, that he had come to this government for such a time as this, and that he was unjust and ungrateful if he did not thus improve his power, or, rather, abuse it. Their hearts are wretchedly hardened who can justify the doing of mischief by their having a power to do it. These priests' business was to examine <hi type="italic">every man that is mad and makes himself a prophet.</hi> God's faithful prophets are here represented as prophets of their own making, usurpers of the office, and lay-intruders, as men that were mad, actuated by some demon, and not divinely inspired, or as distracted men and men in a frenzy. Thus the characters of the false prophets are thrown upon the true ones; and, if this had been indeed their character, they would have deserved to be bound as madmen and punished as pretenders, and therefore he concludes that Jeremiah must be so treated. He does not bid them examine whether Jeremiah could produce any proofs of his mission and could make it to appear that he was not mad. No; that is taken for granted, and, when once he has had a bad name given him, he must be run down of course. 2. He informs them of the letter which Jeremiah had written to the captives (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">He sent unto us in Babylon,</hi> with the authority of a prophet, saying, <hi type="italic">This captivity is long,</hi> and therefore resolve to make the best of it. And what harm was there in this, that it should be objected to him as a crime? The false prophets had formerly said that the captivity would never come, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.3">ch. xiv. 13</reference>. Jeremiah had said that it would come, and the event had already proved him in the right, which obliged them to give credit to him who now said that it would be long, rather than to those who said that it would be short, but had once before been found liars. 3. He demands judgment against him, taking it for granted that he is <hi type="italic">mad,</hi> and <hi type="italic">makes himself a prophet.</hi> He expects that they will order him to be put <hi type="italic">in prison</hi> and <hi type="italic">in the stocks</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.26">v. 26</reference>), that they will thus punish him, and by putting him to disgrace possess the people with prejudices against him, ruin his reputation, and so prevent the giving of any credit to his prophecies at Jerusalem, hoping that, if they could gain that point, the captives in Babylon would not be influenced by him. Nay, he takes upon him to chide Zephaniah for his neglect (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Why hast thou not rebuked and restrained Jeremiah of Anathoth?</hi> See how insolent and imperious these false prophets had grown, that, though they were in captivity, they would give law to the priests who were not only at liberty, but in power. It is common for those that pretend to more knowledge than their neighbours to be thus assuming. Now here is a remarkable instance of the hardness of the hearts of sinners, and it is enough to make us all fear <hi type="italic">lest our hearts be at any time hardened.</hi> For here we find, (1.) That these sinners would not be convinced by the clearest evidence. God had confirmed his word in the mouth of Jeremiah; it had <hi type="italic">taken hold</hi> of them (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.6">Zech. i. 6</reference>); and yet, because he does not prophesy to them the smooth things they desired, they are resolved to look upon him as not duly called to the office of a prophet. None so blind as those that will not see. (2.) That they would not be reclaimed and reformed by the most severe chastisement. They were now sent into a miserable thraldom for <hi type="italic">mocking the messengers of the Lord</hi> and <hi type="italic">misusing his prophets.</hi> This was the sin for which God now contended with them; and yet in <hi type="italic">their distress they trespass yet more against the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.22">2 Chron. xxviii. 22</reference>. This very sin they are notoriously guilty of in their captivity, which shows that afflictions will not of themselves cure men of their sins, unless the grace of God work with them, but will rather exasperate the corruptions they are intended to mortify; so true is that of Solomon (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.22">Prov. xxvii. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">Though thou shouldst bray a fool in a mortar, yet will not his foolishness depart from him.</hi> <div eID="gen17843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17844" type="x-p"/> II. How Jeremiah came to the knowledge of this (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">Zephaniah read this letter in the ears of Jeremiah.</hi> He did not design to do as Shemaiah would have him, but, as it should seem, had a respect for Jeremiah (for we find him employed in messages to him as a <hi type="italic">prophet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">ch. xxi. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">xxxvii. 3</reference>), and therefore protected him. He that continued in his dignity and power stood more in awe of God and his judgments than he that was now a captive. Nay, he made Jeremiah acquainted with the contents of the letter, that he might see what enemies he had even among the captives. Note, It is kindness to our friends to let them know their foes. <div eID="gen17844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17845" type="x-p"/> III. What was the sentence passed upon Shemaiah for writing this letter. God sent him an answer, for to him Jeremiah committed his cause: it was ordered to be sent not to him, but <hi type="italic">to those of the captivity,</hi> who encouraged and countenanced him as if he had been a prophet of God's raising up, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.31-Jer.29.32">v. 31, 32</reference>. Let them know, 1. That Shemaiah had made fools of them. He promised them peace in God's name, but God did not send him; he forged a commission, and counterfeited the broad seal of Heaven to it, and made the people <hi type="italic">to trust in a lie,</hi> and by preaching false comfort to them deprived them of true comfort. Nay, he had not only made fools of them, but, which was worse, he had made traitors of them; he had <hi type="italic">taught rebellion against the Lord,</hi> as Hananiah had done, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.16">ch. xxviii. 16</reference>. And, if vengeance shall be taken on those that rebel, much more on those that teach rebellion by their doctrine and example. 2. That at his end <hi type="italic">he shall also be a fool</hi> (as the expression is, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.11">ch. xvii. 11</reference>); his name and family shall be extinct and shall be buried in oblivion; he shall leave no issue behind him to bear up his name; his pedigree shall end in him: <hi type="italic">He shall not have a man to dwell among this people;</hi> and neither he nor any that come from him shall <hi type="italic">behold the good that I will do for my people.</hi> Note, Those are unworthy to share in God's favours to his church that are not willing to stay his time for them. Shemaiah was angry at Jeremiah's advice to the captives to see to the building up of their families in Babylon, that they might be increased and not diminished, and therefore justly is he written childless there. Those that slight the blessings of God's word deserve to lose the benefit of them. See <reference osisRef="Amos.7.16-Amos.7.17">Amos vii. 16, 17</reference>.  <chapter eID="Jer.29"/> <div eID="gen17845" type="x-p"/>

entries.f09f56c0e21541fc72f86a4ab4dd1c93237c9ec8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10203"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 29</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.29.1-Jer.29.32">Jr 29:1-32</reference>. Letter of Jeremiah to the Captives in Babylon, to Counteract the Assurances Given by the False Prophets of a Speedy Restoration.</title> <div sID="gen18189" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10203"/><hi type="bold">1. residue of the elders--</hi>those still surviving from the time when they were carried to Babylon with Jeconiah; the other elders of the captives had died by either a natural or a violent death. <div eID="gen18189" type="x-p"/>
entries.978c33ea7b358da08ed827f5140d63120fd847b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10204"/><div sID="gen18190" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10204"/><hi type="bold">2. queen--</hi>Nehushta, the queen mother, daughter of Elnathan (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.8">2Ki 24:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.15">15</reference>). (Elnathan, her father, is perhaps the same as the one mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jer.26.22">Jr 26:22</reference>). She reigned jointly with her son.<div eID="gen18190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18191" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">princes--</hi>All the men of authority were taken away lest they should organize a rebellion. Jeremiah wrote his letter while the calamity was still recent, to console the captives under it. <div eID="gen18191" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e8ec946285f28b6012233269fc01fbf85660b8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10205"/><div sID="gen18192" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10205"/><hi type="bold">3. Zedekiah ... sent unto Babylon--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Jer.51.59">Jr 51:59</reference>, Zedekiah himself goes to Babylon; here he sends ambassadors. Whatever was the object of the embassy, it shows that Zedekiah only reigned at the pleasure of the king of Babylon, who might have restored Jeconiah, had he pleased. Hence, Zedekiah permitted Jeremiah's letter to be sent, not only as being led by Hananiah's death to attach greater credit to the prophet's words, but also as the letter accorded with his own wish that the Jews should remain in Chaldea till Jeconiah's death.<div eID="gen18192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hilkiah--</hi>the high priest who found the book of the law in the house of the Lord, and showed it to "Shaphan" the scribe (the same Shaphan probably as here), who showed it to King Josiah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.8">2Ki 22:8</reference>, &c.). The sons of Hilkiah and Shaphan inherited from their fathers some respect for sacred things. So in <reference osisRef="Jer.36.25">Jr 36:25</reference>, "Gemariah" interceded with King Jehoiakim that the prophet's roll should not be burned. <div eID="gen18193" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff82b3cddebb19a9cad69dff9d899a9839d219d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10206"/><div sID="gen18194" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10206"/><hi type="bold">5. Build ... houses--</hi>In opposition to the false prophets' suggestions, who told the captives that their captivity would soon cease, Jeremiah tells them that it will be of long duration, and that therefore they should build houses, as Babylon is to be for long their home. <div eID="gen18194" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3064c42eaf46153b7c698f31950b222b7989c0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10207"/><div sID="gen18195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10207"/><hi type="bold">6. that ye ... be ... not diminished--</hi>It was God's will that the seed of Abraham should not fail; thus consolation is given them, and the hope, though not of an immediate, yet of an ultimate, return. <div eID="gen18195" type="x-p"/>
entries.1031ef4104d145d0d9e6f4fdd8fa8792e5f52130: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10208"/><div sID="gen18196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10208"/>7. (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.10">Ezr 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1">Ro 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.2">1Ti 2:2</reference>). Not only bear the Babylonian yoke patiently, but pray for your masters, that is, while the captivity lasts. God's good time was to come when they were to pray for Babylon's downfall (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.35">Jr 51:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.137.8">Psa 137:8</reference>). They were not to forestall that time. True religion teaches patient submission, not sedition, even though the prince be an unbeliever. In all states of life let us not throw away the comfort we may have, because we have not all we would have. There is here a foretaste of gospel love towards enemies (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">Mt 5:44</reference>). <div eID="gen18196" type="x-p"/>
entries.209c22afcf1d81f0f91a79ef90ab33aee414d67a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10209"/><div sID="gen18197" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10209"/><hi type="bold">8. your dreams which ye caused to be dreamed--</hi>The Latin adage says, "The people wish to be deceived, so let them be deceived." Not mere credulity misleads men, but their own perverse "love of darkness rather than light." It was not priests who originated priestcraft, but the people's own morbid appetite to be deceived; for example, Aaron and the golden calf (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.1-Exod.32.4">Ex 32:1-4</reference>). So the Jews caused or made the prophets to tell them encouraging dreams (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.25">Jr 23:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">Ec 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.2">Zec 10:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.19-John.3.21">Joh 3:19-21</reference>). <div eID="gen18197" type="x-p"/>
entries.412ee0477b7a80d0e1ea7d9feaa7be708d57c3ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10210"/><div sID="gen18198" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10210"/>10. (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.25.11">Jr 25:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">Jr 25:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.2">Da 9:2</reference>). This proves that the seventy years date from Jeconiah's captivity, not from the last captivity. The specification of time was to curb the impatience of the Jews lest they should hasten before God's time.<div eID="gen18198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18199" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good word--</hi>promise of a return. <div eID="gen18199" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad60766a80723c8536052bf0b3b90842c91faaf6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10211"/><div sID="gen18200" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10211"/><hi type="bold">11. I know--</hi>I alone; not the false prophets who know nothing of My purposes, though they pretend to know.<div eID="gen18200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18201" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thoughts ... I think--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.55.9">Is 55:9</reference>). Glancing at the Jews who had no "thoughts of peace," but only of "evil" (misfortune), because they could not conceive how deliverance could come to them. The moral malady of man is twofold--at one time vain confidence; then, when that is disappointed, despair. So the Jews first laughed at God's threats, confident that they should speedily return; then, when cast down from that confidence, they sank in inconsolable despondency.<div eID="gen18201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18202" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">expected end--</hi>literally, "end and expectation," that is, an end, and that such an end as you wish for. Two nouns joined by "and," standing for a noun and adjective. So in <reference osisRef="Jer.36.27">Jr 36:27</reference>, "the roll and the words," that is, the roll of words; <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Ge 3:16</reference>, "sorrow and conception," that is, sorrow in conception. Compare <reference osisRef="Prov.23.18">Pr 23:18</reference>, where, as here "end" means "a happy issue." <div eID="gen18202" type="x-p"/>
entries.253a5b25b90892b158f4f268bca48f32f46a24da: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10212"/><div sID="gen18203" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10212"/>12. Fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.3">Da 9:3</reference>, &c.). When God designs mercy, He puts it into the hearts of His people to pray for the mercy designed. When such a spirit of prayer is poured out, it is a sure sign of coming mercy.<div eID="gen18203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go--</hi>to the temple and other places of prayer: contrasted with their previous sloth as to going to seek God. <div eID="gen18204" type="x-p"/>

entries.91031b70b846a778f262b9d22d9e2488a279ab09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10215"/><div sID="gen18208" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10215"/><hi type="bold">15. Because--</hi>referring not to the preceding words, but to <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">Jr 29:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.11">11</reference>, "Jehovah saith this to you" (that is, the prophecy of the continuance of the captivity seventy years), "because ye have said, The Lord hath raised us up prophets in Babylon," namely, foretelling our speedy deliverance (this their prophecy is supposed, not expressed; accordingly, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.16-Jer.29.19">Jr 29:16-19</reference> contradict this false hope again, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.8">Jr 29:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.21">9, 21</reference>). He, in this fifteenth verse, turns his address from the godly (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.12-Jer.29.14">Jr 29:12-14</reference>) to the ungodly listeners, to false prophets. <div eID="gen18208" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c0a2d787210f40a34e27d0a1a0f0b203b1abf21: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10216"/><div sID="gen18209" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10216"/><hi type="bold">16. people ... in this city ... not gone forth--</hi>So far from your returning to Jerusalem soon, even your brethren still left dwelling there shall themselves also be cast into exile. He mentions "the throne of David," lest they should think that, because David's kingdom was to be perpetual, no severe, though temporary, chastisements could interpose (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.29-Ps.89.36">Psa 89:29-36</reference>). <div eID="gen18209" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1e18760ef246cab7fa8316bd587ba0a16cd0fb1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10217"/><div sID="gen18210" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10217"/><hi type="bold">17. vile figs--</hi>Hebrew, "horrible," or nauseous, from a root, "to regard with loathing" (see <reference osisRef="Jer.24.8">Jr 24:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.24.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen18210" type="x-p"/>
entries.6dd32dc84e5399f27157dea8763602fda9bd287e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10218"/><div sID="gen18211" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10218"/><hi type="bold">18. removed to all ... kingdoms--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.15.4">Jr 15:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.25">De 28:25</reference>).<div eID="gen18211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">curse, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.29.6">Jr 29:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.16">18:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.19.8">19:8</reference>). <div eID="gen18212" type="x-p"/>

Zedekiah--</hi>brother of Zephaniah (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.25">Jr 29:25</reference>), both being sons of Maaseiah; probably of the same family as the false prophet under Ahab in Israel (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.11">1Ki 22:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.24">24</reference>). <div eID="gen18213" type="x-p"/>
entries.a0096d953e83bcae9f8f78bdc22560a5cc135e06: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10220"/><div sID="gen18214" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10220"/><hi type="bold">22. shall be taken ... a curse--</hi>that is, a formula of imprecation.<div eID="gen18214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord make thee like Zedekiah--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.48.20">Ge 48:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.15">Is 65:15</reference>).<div eID="gen18215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">roasted in the fire--</hi>a Chaldean punishment (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.6">Da 3:6</reference>). <div eID="gen18216" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd37df7f9d97a14b1d36e0885120d45437476f9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10221"/><div sID="gen18217" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10221"/><hi type="bold">23. villainy--</hi>literally, "sinful folly" (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.6">Is 32:6</reference>). <div eID="gen18217" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad5859ff1d38b09d8d252eb47f0ebe93894bb81d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10222"/><div sID="gen18218" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10222"/>24-32. A second communication which Jeremiah sent to Babylon, after the messenger who carried his first letter had brought a letter from the false prophet Shemaiah to Zephaniah, &c., condemning Jeremiah and reproving the authorities for not having apprehended him.<div eID="gen18218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Nehelamite--</hi>a name derived either from his father or from a place: alluding at the same time to the Hebrew meaning, "a dreamer" (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.29.8">Jr 29:8</reference>). <div eID="gen18219" type="x-p"/>

entries.951afbd1fad661160678c3c88cbbed3b6b15e582: <div eID="gen30045" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30046" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30047" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30047" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30046" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30048" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains the substance of two letters sent by the prophet to the captives in Babylon. In the first he recommends to them patience and composure under their present circumstances, which were to endure for seventy years, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.1-Jer.29.14">Jer 29:1-14</reference>; in which, however, they should fare better than their brethren who remained behind, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.15-Jer.29.19">Jer 29:15-19</reference>. But, finding little credit given to this message, on account of the suggestions of the false prophets, Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and Zedekiah, the son of Maaseiah, who flattered them with the hopes of a speedy end to their captivity, he sends a second, in which he denounces heavy judgments against those false prophets that deceived them, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.20-Jer.29.23">Jer 29:20-23</reference>; as he did afterwards against Shemaiah the Nehelamite, who had sent a letter of complaint against Jeremiah, in consequence of his message, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.24-Jer.29.32">Jer 29:24-32</reference>. <div eID="gen30048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30049" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30050" type="x-p"/> Now these are the words of the letter - This transaction took place in the first or second year of Zedekiah. It appears that the prophet had been informed that the Jews who had already been carried into captivity had, through the instigations of false prophets, been led to believe that they were to be brought out of their captivity speedily. Jeremiah, fearing that this delusion might induce them to take some hasty steps, ill comporting with their present state, wrote a letter to them, which he entrusted to an embassy which Zedekiah had sent on some political concerns to Nebuchadnezzar. The letter was directed to the elders, priests, prophets, and people who had been carried away captives to Babylon.
entries.b1107d802a3fca8aa72f361931e3e4e9791d9410: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen30050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30051" type="x-p"/> Thus saith the Lord of hosts - This was the commencement of the letter.
entries.80f0481c4522aa88c50d27b37877415c3d24b5aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen30051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30052" type="x-p"/> Build ye houses - Prepare for a long continuance in your present captivity. Provide yourselves with the necessaries of life, and multiply in the land, that ye may become a powerful people.
entries.77f8d3c12546d3ebd399b05e4897c8de256f0a63: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30053" type="x-p"/> Seek the peace of the city - Endeavor to promote, as far as you can, the prosperity of the places in which ye sojourn. Let no disaffection appear in word or act. Nothing can be more reasonable than this. Wherever a man lives and has his nourishment and support, that is his country as long as he resides in it. If things go well with that country, his interest is promoted by the general prosperity, he lives at comparative ease, and has the necessaries of life cheaper; and unless he is in a state of cruel servitude, which does not appear to have been the case with those Israelites to whom the prophet writes, (those of the first captivity), they must be nearly, if not altogether, in as good a state as if they had been in the country that gave them birth. And in this case they were much better off than their brethren now in Judea, who had to contend with famine and war, and scarcely any thing before them but God's curse and extermination.
entries.c3f0f874403496f6ac1b0c2489fed65bbaf28abb: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen30053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30054" type="x-p"/> Neither hearken to your dreams - Rather, dreamers; for it appears there was a class of such persons, who not only had acquired a facility of dreaming themselves, but who undertook to interpret the dreams of others.
entries.6a9cfe7e9672e534eafc04cbcaabe52d346f5027: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen30054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30055" type="x-p"/> For thus saith the Lord - It has been supposed that a very serious transposition of verses has taken place here; and it has been proposed to read after <reference osisRef="Jer.29.9">Jer 29:9</reference> the sixteenth to the nineteenth inclusive; then the tenth, and on to the fourteenth inclusive; then the twentieth, the fifteenth, the twenty-first, and the rest regularly to the end. <div eID="gen30055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30056" type="x-p"/> That after seventy years be accomplished - לפי מלאת lephi meloth, "at the mouth of the accomplishment," or "fill to the mouth." Seventy years is the measure which must be filled; - fill this to the brim; - complete this measure, and then you shall be visited and released. The whole seventy must be completed; expect no enlargement before that time.
entries.23418c341be83e0d025bbbb97233c09dcdd9f4a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen30056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30057" type="x-p"/> Thoughts of peace - Here God gives them to understand, <div eID="gen30057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30058" type="x-p"/> 1. That his love was moved towards them. <div eID="gen30058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30059" type="x-p"/> 2. That he would perform his good word, his promises often repeated, to them. <div eID="gen30059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30060" type="x-p"/> 3. That for the fulfillment of these they must pray, seek, and search. <div eID="gen30060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30061" type="x-p"/> 4. That he would hearken, and they should find him; provided, <div eID="gen30061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30062" type="x-p"/> 5. They sought him with their whole heart, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10-Jer.29.13">Jer 29:10-13</reference>.
entries.e11b231d6d3bc92aa3f3db6ecf80fc60c974951d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen30062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30063" type="x-p"/> I will gather you from all the nations - A quotation from <reference osisRef="Deu.30.3">Deu 30:3</reference>, and see also <reference osisRef="Deu.4.7">Deu 4:7</reference>.
entries.4d51d213adf5b9b36628d61fefe71334f8f4bf92: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen30063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30064" type="x-p"/> Because ye have said - The Septuagint very properly insert this verse between the twentieth and the twenty-first, and thus the connection here is not disturbed, and the connection below completed.
entries.15052210d8b7017e67ec865d4717bdfd6cdf689a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen30064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30065" type="x-p"/> Behold, I will send upon them the sword - Do not envy the state of Zedekiah who sits on the throne of David, nor that of the people who are now in the land whence ye have been carried captive, (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.16">Jer 29:16</reference>), for "I will send the sword, the pestilence, and the famine upon them;" and afterwards shall cause them to be carried into a miserable captivity in all nations, (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.18">Jer 29:18</reference>); but ye see the worst of your own case, and you have God's promise of enlargement when the proper time is come. The reader will not forget that the prophet is addressing the captives in Babylon.
entries.4ff3da05b2b2fe3b1eee3dc05ca2539e7050363c: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen30065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30066" type="x-p"/> Hear ye therefore the word - Dr. Blayney thinks there were two letters written by the prophet to the captives in Babylon, and that the first ends with this verse. That having heard, on the return of the embassy (Elasah and Gemariah, whom Zedekiah had sent to Babylon, and to whom the prophet entrusted the above letter, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.3">Jer 29:3</reference>), that the captives had not received his advises favourably, because they were deceived by false prophets among them, who promised them a speedier deliverance, he therefore wrote a second letter, beginning with the fifteenth verse, and going on with the twenty-first, etc., in which he denounces God's judgments on three of the chief of those, Ahab, Zedekiah, and Shemaiah.
entries.44a434350730f6fcc8fe5fdb64c0e70f06760b83: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen30066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30067" type="x-p"/> He shall slay them before your eyes - Nebuchadnezzar would be led by political reasons to punish these pretended prophets, as their predictions tended to make his Israelitish subjects uneasy and disaffected, and might excite them to rebellion. He therefore slew them; two of them, it appears, he burnt alive, viz., Ahab and Zedekiah, who are supposed by the rabbins to be the two elders who endeavored to seduce Susanna, see <reference osisRef="Jer.29.23">Jer 29:23</reference>. Burning alive was a Chaldean punishment, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.6">Dan 3:6</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Amo.2.1">Amo 2:1</reference>. From them other nations borrowed it.
entries.054291f25345a72b71a274179f6a1e1e3a318c5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen30067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30068" type="x-p"/> Have committed adultery with their neighbors' wives - This is supposed to refer to the case of Susanna. See above.
entries.ae9bbd99ac52d5fca72ceefaffc46f7c91476c6f: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen30068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30069" type="x-p"/> Speak to Shemaiah - Zephaniah was the second priest, sagan, or chief priest's deputy, and Seraiah, high priest, when Jerusalem was taken. See <reference osisRef="Jer.52.24">Jer 52:24</reference>. Shemaiah directs his letter to the former, and tells him that God had appointed him to supply the place of the high priest, who was probably then absent. His name was either Azariah or Seraiah his son, but called Jehoiada from the remarkable zeal and courage of that pontiff. See the passages in the margin. - Dodd. After the taking of Jerusalem, Zephaniah was put to death by Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, see <reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">Jer 37:3</reference>. The history of Jehoiada may be seen <reference osisRef="2Kgs.11.3">2Kgs 11:3</reference>, etc.
entries.e6aa379d9198e63ee1153e8133f251e43077e03a: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen30069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30070" type="x-p"/> For every man that is mad, and maketh himself a prophet - Mad, משגע meshugga, in ecstatic rapture; such as appeared in the prophets, whether true or false, when under the influence, the one of God, the other of a demon. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.11">2Kgs 9:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.9.7">Hos 9:7</reference>.
entries.f7a96ca17f04603491b56b5ce80cb4f73ccb8f2f: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen30070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30071" type="x-p"/> I will punish Shemaiah - <div eID="gen30071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30072" type="x-p"/> 1. He shall have no posterity to succeed him. <div eID="gen30072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30073" type="x-p"/> 2. His family, i.e., relations, etc., shall not be found among those whom I shall bring back from captivity. <div eID="gen30073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30074" type="x-p"/> 3. Nor shall he himself see the good that I shall do for my people. <div eID="gen30074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30075" type="x-p"/> And all this shall come upon him and his because he hath taught rebellion against the Lord. He excited the people to reject Jeremiah, and to receive the lying words of the false prophets; and these led them to rebel.  <chapter eID="Jer.29"/> <div eID="gen30075" type="x-p"/>

entries.9e2360a21aff0fac49cb9b2ab9723304cad62e23: <reference osisRef="Jer.29.1-Jer.29.3">Jer 29:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen14171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14172" type="x-p"/> A Letter from Jeremiah to the Captives in Babylon, together with Threatenings against their False Prophets. - As in Jerusalem, so too in Babylon the predictions of the false prophets fostered a lively hope that the domination of Nebuchadnezzar would not last long, and that the return of the exiles to their fatherland would soon come about. The spirit of discontent thus excited must have exercised an injurious influence on the fortunes of the captives, and could not fail to frustrate the aim which the chastisement inflicted by God was designed to work out, namely, the moral advancement of the people. Therefore Jeremiah makes use of an opportunity furnished by an embassy sent by King Zedekiah to Babel, to address a letter to the exiles, exhorting them to yield with submission to the lot God had assigned to them. He counsels them to prepare, by establishing their households there, for a long sojourn in Babel, and to seek the welfare of that country as the necessary condition of their own. They must not let themselves be deceived by the false prophets’ idle promises of a speedy return, since God will not bring them back and fulfil His glorious promises till after seventy years have passed (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.4-Jer.29.14">Jer 29:4-14</reference>). Then he tells them that sore judgments are yet in store for King Zedekiah and such as have been left in the land (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.15-Jer.29.20">Jer 29:15-20</reference>); and declares that some of their false prophets shall perish miserably (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.21-Jer.29.32">Jer 29:21-32</reference>).<hi type="italic">Heading and Introduction.</hi> - The following circular is connected, in point of outward form, with the preceding discourses against the false prophets in Jerusalem by means of the words: <hi type="italic">"And these are the words of the letter,"</hi> etc. The words of the letter, i.e., the main contents of the letter, since it was not transcribed, but given in substance. "Which the prophet Jeremiah sent from Jerusalem unto the residue of the elders of the captives, and to the priests and prophets, and to the whole people, which Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon." "The residue of the elders," Hitz. and Graf understand of those elders who were not at the same time priests or prophets. On this Näg. pronounces: "It is impossible that they can be right, for then 'the residue of the elders of the captivity' must have stood after the priests and prophets." And though we hear of elders of the priests, there is no trace in the O.T. of elders of the prophets. Besides, the elders, whenever they are mentioned along with the priests, are universally the elders of the people. Thus must we understand the expression here also. "The residue of the elders" can only be the remaining, i.e., still surviving, elders of the exiles, as יתר is used also in <reference osisRef="Jer.39.9">Jer 39:9</reference> for those still in life. But there is no foundation for the assumption by means of which Gr. seeks to support his interpretation, namely, that the place of elders that died was immediately filled by new appointments, so that the council of the elders must always have been regarded as a whole, and could not come to be a residue or remnant. Jeremiah could not possibly have assumed the existence of such an organized governing authority, since in this very letter he exhorts them to set about the establishment of regular system in their affairs. The date given in <reference osisRef="Jer.29.2">Jer 29:2</reference> : <hi type="italic">"after that Jechoniah the king, and the sovereign lady, and the courtiers, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem, the workmen and smiths, were gone away from Jerusalem,"</hi> points to the beginning of Zedekiah’s reign, to the first or second year of it. With this the advice given to the captives in the letter harmonizes well, namely, the counsel to build houses, plant gardens, etc.; since this makes it clear that they had not been long there. The despatch of this letter is usually referred to the fourth year of Zedekiah’s reign, because in <reference osisRef="Jer.28.1">Jer 28:1</reference> this year is specified. But the connection in point of matter between the present chapter and Jer 28 does not necessarily imply their contemporaneousness, although that is perfectly possible; and the fact that, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.51.59">Jer 51:59</reference>, Zedekiah himself undertook a journey to Babylon in the fourth year of his reign, does not exclude the possibility of an embassy thither in the same year. The going away from Jerusalem is the emigration to Babylon; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.24.1">Jer 24:1</reference>, 2Ki 24:15. הגּבירה, the queen-mother, see on Jer 13:18. סריסים are the officials of the court; not necessarily eunuchs. Both words are joined to the king, because these stood in closest relations to him. Then follows without copula the second class of emigrants, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem, i.e., the heads of the tribes, septs, and families of the nation. The artisans form the third class. This disposes of the objections raised by Mov. and Hitz. against the genuineness of the words "princes of Judah and Jerusalem," their objections being based on the false assumption that these words were an exposition of "courtiers." Cf. against this, 2Ki 24:15, where along with the סריסים the heads of tribes and families are comprehended under the head of אוּלי הארץ. Jer 29:3. "By the hand" of <hi type="italic">Elasah</hi> is dependent on "sent," Jer 29:1. The men by whom Jeremiah sent the letter to Babylon are not further known. <hi type="italic">Shaphan</hi> is perhaps the same who is mentioned in Jer 26:24. We have no information as to the aim of the embassy.
entries.6561d38b698d9d3054c7a45f74e7d36d98bb5caa: <reference osisRef="Jer.29.4-Jer.29.14">Jer 29:4-14</reference> <div eID="gen14172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14173" type="x-p"/> At <reference osisRef="Jer.29.4">Jer 29:4</reference> the contents of the letter begin. Jeremiah warns the people to prepare for a lengthened sojourn in Babylonia, and exhorts them to settle down there. Jer 29:5. <hi type="italic">"Build houses and dwell (therein), and plant gardens and eat the fruit of them. </hi> Jer 29:6. <hi type="italic">Take wives and beget sons and daughters, and take for your sons wives and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters; and increase there and not diminish. </hi> Jer 29:7. <hi type="italic">And seek the safety of the city whither I have carried you captive, and pray for it to Jahveh, and in its safety shall be safety to you."</hi> The imperatives "increase and not diminish" give the consequence of what has been said just before. "The city whither I have carried you captive" is not precisely Babylon, but every place whither separate companies of the exiles have been transported.
